Heritage sites by state

Heritage sites in Meghalaya: root bridges, monoliths and caves

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

Meghalaya's heritage is mostly living and made with nature: the living root bridges of the Khasi and Jaintia hills (on India's UNESCO tentative list), the Nartiang monoliths, the Jaintia rajas' summer capital, sacred groves such as Mawphlang, and long cave systems. The state has no inscribed UNESCO World Heritage Site.

We design study tours to Meghalaya's root bridges, monoliths and sacred groves for groups on request.

Why Meghalaya's heritage is different

Meghalaya is home mainly to three communities: the Khasi and the Jaintia (Pnar) in the centre and east, and the Garo in the west. All three are matrilineal, with descent and often property passing through the mother's line. Much of their heritage is not a building but a practice: how forests are protected, how bridges are grown, how the dead are remembered with stone. Our guides to anthropology and tribal India and intangible cultural heritage explain this way of looking at heritage.

Before British rule, the Khasi and Jaintia hills were divided among small states (hima), each with a ruler (syiem) chosen within particular clans, and the Jaintia kingdom also held land in the Sylhet plains. Many of these institutions continue in some form.

Museums in Meghalaya

  • Don Bosco Centre for Indigenous Cultures, Shillong. Seven floors on the peoples and cultures of the north-east.
  • Meghalaya State Museum, Shillong. Ethnographic and archaeological collections.
  • Wankhar Butterfly Museum, Shillong. Private natural history collection.

Living root bridges

Living root bridges are made by training the aerial roots of the Indian rubber fig (Ficus elastica) across streams, using bamboo or areca palm trunks as guides, until the roots grow strong enough to carry people. A bridge can take a decade or more to become usable and then strengthens for many years. They are found in many villages in the Khasi and Jaintia hills; the double-decker bridge at Nongriat, near Sohra (Cherrapunji), is the best known.

The Jingkieng Jri living root bridge cultural landscape is on India's tentative list for World Heritage. That means it has been proposed, not inscribed. These bridges are also community infrastructure, so visitors should keep to paths, avoid climbing on roots and pay attention to village rules.

Monoliths and megaliths

Meghalaya has one of India's largest living megalithic traditions. Standing stones (menhirs, called mawbynna) and flat table stones (dolmens) were raised to commemorate ancestors, mark clan land and record important events. Nartiang, in the West Jaintia Hills, has a large group of monoliths, including one of the tallest standing stones in the region, traditionally linked to the Jaintia rulers. Nartiang also has a Durga temple of the Jaintia rajas, who used it as a summer capital.

Monoliths line the roads near Sohra, Mawphlang and Laitlum, and some villages still raise memorial stones. Archaeologists find it hard to date the older stones directly, so ages are often given broadly. Our session on burials and bioarchaeology explains how megaliths are studied elsewhere in India.

Sacred groves and caves

Sacred groves (law kyntang) are forests protected by custom, where cutting trees or removing anything is forbidden. Mawphlang, near Shillong, is the best known and has monoliths inside; visits are usually with a local guide. Such groves have preserved plant species and are a good example of conservation by tradition.

Meghalaya has some of the longest cave systems in India, including Krem Liat Prah and Siju in the Garo Hills. A stalagmite from Mawmluh cave, near Sohra, was used to define the Meghalayan Age, the latest stage of the Holocene, starting about 4,200 years ago, which was ratified by the International Commission on Stratigraphy in 2018. Our talk on climate change and ancient settlements explains why that drought event matters for early civilisations.

Shillong and the Garo Hills

Shillong, the capital of Assam until 1972, has colonial churches, the old Assam Secretariat area, Ward's Lake and the Don Bosco Centre for Indigenous Cultures, a large museum on the north-east. The Garo Hills have villages with traditional bachelors' dormitories (nokpante) and the Wangala harvest festival. Archaeologists have reported Stone Age tools from the Garo Hills, and excavations around Sohra have found evidence of iron smelting in the past.

Festivals and living traditions

Festivals in Meghalaya follow the agricultural and religious calendar. Behdienkhlam, held by the Pnar at Jowai around July, is a ritual to drive away disease, with decorated structures carried and plunged into a pool. Shad Suk Mynsiem, the Khasi dance of thanksgiving held in Shillong in spring, and Nongkrem, a dance linked to the hima of Khyrim at Smit, are major public events. Wangala, the Garo harvest festival, honours the sun deity Saljong with drums and dance.

Many people in Meghalaya are Christian, and churches built since the 19th century are part of the heritage too, as is the work of Welsh missionaries who wrote the Khasi language in Roman script. Indigenous religion, Niam Khasi and Niamtre among the Pnar, continues alongside, and the sacred groves and memorial stones belong to that tradition.

For visitors, the rule is simple: ask before entering, ask before photographing, and follow local custom. Our lecture on culture and heritage helps groups think about what it means to visit someone else's living heritage.

Planning a heritage visit to Meghalaya

Shillong is the base for Mawphlang, Sohra and the root bridges, Nartiang and Jowai. The Garo Hills (Tura) are a separate trip. The monsoon is very heavy; October to April is easier for walking, and root bridge treks involve many steps. Ask locally before visiting sacred groves or memorial stones.

Meghalaya trips are planned with each group. We design a study tour for your group and private journeys, and can give a lecture on living heritage or community stewardship before you go.

Questions people ask

Are the living root bridges a UNESCO site?

Not yet. The Jingkieng Jri living root bridge cultural landscape is on India's tentative list for World Heritage, which means it has been proposed but not inscribed. Meghalaya has no inscribed World Heritage Site as of October 2026.

What are the Nartiang monoliths?

Nartiang, in the West Jaintia Hills, has a large group of standing and table stones linked to the Jaintia rulers, who had a summer capital there. The stones commemorated ancestors and events, and include some of the tallest in the region.

How are living root bridges made?

Villagers guide the aerial roots of the Indian rubber fig across a stream using bamboo or palm trunks. Over a decade or more the roots thicken and interlock into a bridge that grows stronger with time.

Can Talaash Heritage plan a study tour to Meghalaya?

Yes, on request. We design study tours for schools, colleges and adult groups, for example Shillong, Sohra, Nartiang and Mawphlang, with a lecture on living heritage or climate and ancient settlements before the trip.
